newsitem.title: UK: Brady vs Eurobonds - are yields on collision course?.
newsitem.headline: Brady vs Eurobonds - are yields on collision course?.

text.p: Emerging market debt yields reached all-time lows earlier this week but they still have a long way to go to catch up with those in the Eurobond market.
For many countries, Brady debt trades a full percentage point above where Eurobonds of a similar maturity trade, despite yield convergence in recent months.
"It is inexplicable, really," said Nick Blakey, head of emerging market Eurobond trading at UBS. "There is a wrongly-held feeling that Eurobonds carry a lower level of risk," he said.
The Brady bond market, so-called after former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, was created in 1989 in an attempt to solve the emerging market bank debt crisis.
Defaulted debt was repackaged with U.S. Treasuries to create new collateralised instruments.

"Brady and Eurobond yields are coming closer as Brady bonds lose some of their stigma, and as emerging market economies become stronger," said Richard Luddington, head of emerging market debt syndicate at J.P. Morgan in London.
"Investors are now looking beyond collateral and want to take the risk of individual countries," he said.
Mexico's global bonds, issued in exchange for Brady paper, are a prime example of this trend.
In May Mexico launched a ground-breaking $1.75 billion 30-year global bond in exchange for collateralised par and discount Brady bonds.
The deal, launched at 552 b.p. over Treasuries and now trading at around 470 b.p. over, was followed by a $1.0 billion 20-year issue on Monday.
"Large U.S. institutions are moving into the emerging markets in search of yield," said a syndicate manager at a European bank.

"They are interested in long-dated, liquid deals, and Mexico's 20- and 30-year global bonds tap into this demand." He added demand for the globals was pronounced because they are the only way to get invest purely in Mexican long-term debt.
The size of the new emerging market globals is also key.
"Brady bonds were always considered preferable because of liquidity. If you can get that liquidity in a Eurobond or global bond, the argument is much weaker," a trader said.
As emerging market sovereigns extend maturities in the Eurobond market, the difference between their yields and those of Brady bonds is highlighted, dealers said.
For instance, last week's 650 million mark seven-year bond issued by Venezuela came at 440 basis points over Bunds, and quickly tightened to 400 b.p. over.
Its uncollaterlised Brady debt conversion bonds, or DCBs, which mature in 2007 but have an average life of 6.25 years, yield 520 b.p. over Treasuries.

Argentina's has a similar story. Its uncollateralised floating rate bonds, or FRBs, maturing in 2005 but with an average life of 5.6 years, trade at 520 b.p. over. Its 2003 dollar Eurobond, which has a 7.25 year-maturity, yields only 410 b.p. above U.S. government paper.

"The situation differs from country to country, with the Philippine yields already nearly the same (as Eurobonds of similar maturities), but in general Brady bonds yield more," said a London-based debt trader.
Blakey at UBS said: "Eventully Brady bonds will trade at similar spreads to Eurobonds at the longer maturities".
More supply is likely to be taken out of the Brady bond market as borrowers seek to refinance the debt more cheaply in the international bond markets and release the collateral to repay debt.
"The exchanges that have been done and the expectation of further exchanges will serve to underpin spreads," said J.P. Morgan's Luddington.
The Philippines is in the process of converting $1.9 billion of debt, Brazil is said to be actively buying Brady bonds in the secondary market and Argentina is rumoured to be eyeing a swap.
Further supply is being taken out of the Brady bond market as banks take advantage of the arbitrage between the two sectors and repackage debt to sell into the Eurobond market.
"The repackaged deals have the same credit risk as a Eurobond, showing there should be no difference between uncollateralised Bradys and Eurobonds," said a trader at a European bank here.
HSBC Trinkaus issued an 50 million mark Eurobond backed by Venezuelan Bradys in July, which was followed by a 75 million mark issue of repackaged Argentina Bradys in September.
